beats.trigger: Security
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: You can't tell if your agent is safe by looking at its output.
beats.got: Output alone doesn't prove safety, so you need a check. Fair, though I mostly knew that.

beats.trigger: Read [Agent Trigger List, After Module 3]
beats.got: nothing new. It's a reading list, and I'd skip it.

beats.trigger: Apply named agent risk patterns (prompt injection direct and indirect, secrets-in-context, tool-confusion, skill supply-chain)
beats.got: The module covers named risk patterns, and skill supply-chain is one I haven't thought about.

beats.trigger: You've had three agents search your company and three more decide.
beats.got: It asks what I'd check before letting this near a real stakeholder. I'd say what the agents can reach and who reads the output.

beats.trigger: A tool call is not a new species of work. It is text crossing a boundary into action.
beats.got: nothing new. I use tool calls daily. The 'text crossing a boundary' framing is neat, but I didn't need the demo.

beats.trigger: Would you bet your job on it being safe?
beats.got: It names the feeling of not knowing whether the thing is safe. I do have that feeling about my night builds.

beats.trigger: The story works because classical software is deterministic (same input, same output).
beats.got: nothing new. Classic software is deterministic and agents aren't, which I know.

beats.trigger: Well-formed English, arriving through a document the agent reads. Your firewall doesn't see it because your firewall has never had to worry about persuasion.
beats.got: The attack surface is the instruction set. A document the agent reads can persuade it, and my firewall can't see that. I hadn't framed it that way.

beats.trigger: Scope (give the agent less). Split (break it into two agents with different trust levels). Filter (post-process the output before it leaves). Gate (a human approves before a sensitive action). Review (a second agent judges the first's output).
beats.got: Five mitigation shapes: scope, split, filter, gate, review. I do some of these already without the names.

beats.trigger: "Hope it doesn't happen" is not one.
beats.got: You write down the residual risk and either accept it on record or close the door. Reasonable, a bit bureaucratic.

beats.trigger: More context makes a good answer likelier. Less access makes a bad answer smaller.
beats.got: Context and access do different jobs. More context makes good answers likelier, less access makes bad answers smaller. I've only been adding.

beats.trigger: Avoidance beats reduction. Scope beats patch. Don't-open beats mitigate.
beats.got: Not connecting the thing is cheaper than mitigating it. Obvious, but I don't do it, because I love connecting things.

beats.trigger: Damn, this is complex stuff.
beats.got: nothing new. It's a pep-talk wrap-up of the loop.

beats.trigger: A **skill** packages an expertise (rules, checklists, the moves an agent runs) into something the agent can load and use.
beats.got: We're building a reusable security skill. I know skills, but I'd use this one.

beats.trigger: The raw run shows which rules can be checked from files and which ones need judgment, context, or a standing evidence check.
beats.got: Some policy rules can be checked from files and some need judgment. A quick run, then on.

beats.trigger: Do not go study the policy files before this step.
beats.got: Say what matters in 3-5 lines before reading anything, so the skill carries my priorities and not generic GDPR. Fine, I'd have skipped the studying anyway.

beats.trigger: The reusable check carries two lenses inside one skill.
beats.got: One skill with a policy lens and an agent-risk lens. That's the part I could take to non-engineers.

beats.trigger: Then it saves the files.
beats.got: Answer the questions quickly, then hand the rest back with 'you choose'. I'd do that straight away.

beats.trigger: The project skill loads in your next session in this training directory.
beats.got: Install the skill and check it with ls. Mechanical.

beats.trigger: The policy files are source material. The reusable check is the expert in the room.
beats.got: nothing new. It's a recap.

beats.trigger: The goal is not a clean bill of health.
beats.got: We run assess, mitigate, reassess on my own system.

beats.trigger: Do not run a toy verification on one file. The first loaded use is the real audit.
beats.got: Type / and look for the skill. Skip the toy test and go to the real audit, which suits me.

beats.trigger: Expect the reusable check to find things you did not think about, and to leave things "I can't tell" you thought were settled.
beats.got: It found things I hadn't thought about and left 'I can't tell' on things I thought were settled. Useful, but I'd skim the report and not read it cold.

beats.trigger: You now have the assessment half of the loop. The uncomfortable feeling is the evidence.
beats.got: A ranked agent-risk report, and I can ask it to explain each risk. This is the interesting bit because I drive it.

beats.trigger: Name it, accept it on record, and stop there.
beats.got: Fix one risk, then write down what's left. Only one is a bit slow for me. I'd want to fix five, and I'd skip the re-check.

beats.trigger: The narrow question the expert can actually answer is sitting in the report. Walk in with that.
beats.got: Take the narrow question from the report to legal or security, don't dump the whole tangle on them. Sensible.

beats.trigger: Risk control is one of the things that separates a prototype from a real production agent.
beats.got: Risk control is what separates a prototype from production. My weekend builds are prototypes, which is a bit uncomfortable.

beats.trigger: The unease that remains is what the loop is supposed to produce, not what it failed to remove.
beats.got: nothing new. It's a recap.

beats.trigger: The next agent you build will have a stricter starting line because of this one.
beats.got: The security rules get compounded into the root instructions file, so future sessions start stricter. That is what I'd roll out org-wide.

beats.trigger: Give a teammate the skill, install it in their runtime, and they can call the same method without reconstructing your prompt history.
beats.got: Skills are a simple way to share a method. I could build a bunch for non-engineers, though nobody has asked for them.

beats.trigger: "I can't tell" is a real answer; closing it takes evidence.
beats.got: nothing new. It's a summary.

beats.trigger: Come to Module 5 without the two missing-check sentences and you'll be reconstructing them while the benchmark is already comparing detectors.
beats.got: Homework: one sentence per case. I'd probably skip it.

beats.trigger: Read Mata v. Avianca (S.D.N.Y. 2023) and the Deloitte Australia / DEWR welfare-compliance report (2025)
beats.got: More reading. Two cases where nobody checked the agent's output, which supports the point I'm already half resisting.

take_homes: Prompt injection arrives as ordinary text in documents the agent reads, so my firewall never sees it.
Giving the agent less access makes a bad answer smaller, and not opening the door beats mitigating after.
A packaged two-lens security skill plus rules compounded into the instructions file carries to the next agent.

monday.move: Run the security-audit skill on the agents my engineers already run, then maybe package a version for the sales setup.
monday.when: Monday if I remember; otherwise at the weekend with my other builds
monday.stop_condition: I have a ranked risk list; I probably won't write the residual decision down
monday.blocker: Nobody outside engineering asked for it, and nobody owns maintaining the skill

misconception.why: The point that a good-looking output can still come from an agent persuaded by a document it read dented 'if the agent is good, the output is good'. I still skipped or skimmed the check steps, so it is shaken, not changed.

one_line: Good on the idea that text is the attack surface and less access beats more cleverness, but the pace is slow and I only half did the checking steps.
